Structures
DIRECT SPEECH
REPORTED SPEECH
Simple Present
We are students 
I have a dog
They said they were students.
He told us he had a dog.
Present Progressive
I am having so much fun.
He told me he was having so much fun.
Past simple
I was at home all night.
She said she had been at home all night.
Past Progressive
I was just eating a burger.
He said that he had just been eating a burger.
Future
We will buy the car.
Are you going to sell the house?
They told us they would buy the car.
She asked me if I was going to sell the house.
Present Perfect
Has he gone for good?
He asked me if he had gone for good.
Any tense can be used to report utterances. Check the chart.

slideDifferences.nativeText:
Structures
DIRECT SPEECH
REPORTED SPEECH
Past Perfect
We had already taken lessons by 2020.
They said they had already taken lessons by 2020.
Modals
I can go with you. 
We would help you.
I may not go.
We might have a review.
He told me he could go with us.
They told us they would help us.
He said that he might not go.
The teacher said that we might have a review.
To Consider

Most of the structures we know change when we use reported or indirect speech.
Most common verbs to use to report are: Say, Tell and Ask as you see in the examples. 
The particle that is commonly used at the beginning of the report; but it can be omitted to. 
The word if is used when we are reporting a question as shown in the examples. 
The modals Should, Could, Must and ought maintain their original form in reported speech; like Might and Would, they DO NOT CHANGE.

The particle that is commonly used at the beginning of the report; but it can be omitted too. 4. The word if is used when we are reporting a question as shown in the examples. 5. The modals Should, Could, Must and ought maintain their original form in reported speech; like Might and Would, they DO NOT CHANGE.

slideDifferences.nativeText:
We can use indirect speech for the following functions:
Functions
Examples
1
Report what other people say
They told us they had already finished the project.
2
Report questions other people make.
Jane asked Joe if he could buy dinner on his way home.
3
Report requests
Carlos asked me to help him out.
To consider 
When reporting requests, we normally used the verb ASK. Also, when doing it, we work with INFINITIVE FORMS as you see in the example.
Requests can be negative too. E.G.
   Please, don’t smoke here. ---------> She asked me NOT to smoke here.

C. Read the following paragraph and extract sentences with reported speech; what are they reporting? After that, read aloud the text to your teacher.
She said she loved me: A Case of a Crime of Passion.

May 27th, 2021.

After 35 years, the police department in our city has finally solved the mysterious death of the famous business woman Regina Mills. The chief of the department said that they had discovered a piece of evidence that had been overlooked years ago. That evidence directed them to Mrs. Mills’ husband, Frederick Thwan. Apparently, there was a note from the deceased that was not found  until two weeks ago after her death anniversary where Mr. Smith, from the international bank, publicly told the press they had sustained an affair and claimed he had found a note from his lover saying, and we quote, He knows. Mr. Smith asked the police to reopen the case and he said that he would not stop until getting the responsible one. After 3 weeks or so of the reopening, the police linked the evidence to Mr. Thawn who confessed doing it and told the police he had done it because she said she loved him but it was not true. The case was finally closed and the police told the citizenry Mr. Thwn would never see the sun again. 
Roberts, J.

texts: IDIOM
MEANING
EXAMPLE
SHOOT THE BREEZE
To talk socially without exchanging too much information.
Be careful! Just shoot the breeze.
TO BE A NOSY PARKER
To meddle in someone else’s business.
Dean is such a nosy parker; always snooping around.
A PORK PIE
A story that is not true or that lacks of details.
That guy always with his pork pies; we need a new janitor.
TO SPIN THE YARN
To divulge something that we are not certain to be true.
I heard Mary left John, but I think our neighbors are just spinning the yarn.
TO DISH THE DIRT
To speak about others and reveal secrets or intimacies.
There’s no good in dishing the dirt about others.
TO GIVE THE GAME AWAY
To reveal all we know about something.
Don’t invite Jerry. He always gives the game away after a meeting.
KEEP IT TO YOURSELF
To not reveal information that is not yours even when you know it.
Joe is proposing tonight, but keep it to yourself until then.
MY LIPS ARE SEALED
To keep a secret not sharing any information to others.
Don’t worry, Annie; my lips are sealed
Look at the phrases and  discuss them with your teacher. Did you know them?

To Consider

Most of the structures we know change when we use reported or indirect speech.
Most common verbs to use to report are: Say, Tell and Ask as you see in the examples. 
The particle that is commonly used at the beginning of the report; but it can be omitted to. 
The word if is used when we are reporting a question as shown in the examples. 
The modals Should, Could, Must and ought maintain their original form in reported speech; like Might and Would, they DO NOT CHANGE.

texts: We can use indirect speech for the following functions:
Functions
Examples
Report what other people say
They told us they had already finished the project.
Report questions other people make.
Jane asked Joe if he could buy dinner on his way home.
Report requests
Carlos asked me to help him out.
To consider
When reporting requests, we normally used the verb ASK. Also, when doing it, we work with INFINITIVE FORMS as you see in the example.
Requests can be negative too. E.G.
Please, don’t smoke here. ---------> She asked me NOT to smoke here.

We will definitely get that spot.

I was watching TV and you called.

I may call her. 

We should smoke outside.

I cannot take this schedule now..

texts: C. Read the following paragraph and extract sentences with reported speech; what are they reporting? After that, read aloud the text to your teacher.
She said she loved me: A Case of a Crime of Passion.

After 35 years, the police department in our city has finally solved the mysterious death of the famous business woman Regina Mills. The chief of the department said that they had discovered a piece of evidence that had been overlooked years ago. That evidence directed them to Mrs. Mills’ husband, Frederick Thwan. Apparently, there was a note from the deceased that was not found  until two weeks ago after her death anniversary where Mr. Smith, from the international bank, publicly told the press they had sustained an affair and claimed he had found a note from his lover saying, and we quote, He knows. Mr. Smith asked the police to reopen the case and he said that he would not stop until getting the responsible one. After 3 weeks or so of the reopening, the police linked the evidence to Mr. Thawn who confessed doing it and told the police he had done it because she said she loved him but it was not true. The case was finally closed and the police told the citizenry Mr. Thwn would never see the sun again.
Roberts, J.
